extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (or readers) learning introductory combinatorics and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Elementary counting methods (multiplication/addition/subtraction principles), factorials, permutations, k-permutations (P(n,k)), combinations/binomial coefficients, Pascal's triangle, and the binomial theorem — as taught in an introductory discrete math/proof textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When a construction can be carried out in a sequence of steps with a fixed number of choices at each step, the total number of constructions is the product of the number of choices for each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout to count lists and arrangements (e.g., computing n(n−1)(n−2)··· when filling successive positions). Examples: counting non-repetitive lists, deriving P(n,k) via n·(n−1)·...·(n−k+1), computing 7! as 7·6·5·4·3·2·1. Implicit in counting arrangements of cards, books on a shelf, and filling password characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of possibilities is a disjoint union of several types, the total number of possibilities is the sum of the counts for each type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to combine mutually exclusive cases. Example: number of lineups that are either all red cards or all clubs = P(26,5) + P(13,5). Also used when partitioning by parity or number of 1's in binary strings and then summing counts for each allowed k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction Principle (Counting by Complement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count items with a property, count the total number of items and subtract those that lack the property (|U − X| = |U| − |X|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when "at least one" or complement conditions are easier to count. Example: number of length-7 lists (with repetition allowed) that contain at least one repeated letter = |U| − |X| where |U| = 7^7 and |X| = 7! (the non-repetitive lists). Also used to count integers with at least one repeated digit by complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 3.1 — Factorial n!
rubrics_metrics.description: If n is a non-negative integer, then n! is the number of lists of length n that can be made from n symbols, without repetition. Thus 0! = 1 and 1! = 1. If n > 1, then n! = n(n − 1)(n − 2) · · · 3 · 2 · 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factorial counts permutations of an n-element set. Examples: 4! = 24, 7! = 5040. Important identities: recurrence n! = n·(n−1)! (Equation 3.1), and explanation why 0! = 1 (empty list and recurrence consistency). Examples show students often mistakenly think 0! = 0; text explains why that is wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation (arrangement) of a set
rubrics_metrics.description: A permutation of a set is an arrangement of all of the set's elements in a row, i.e., a list without repetition that uses every element of the set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of permutations of an n-element set = n!. Examples: permutations of {1,2,3} are 123,132,213,231,312,321 (3! = 6). Interpretation: arranging books on a shelf or ordering contestants is a permutation problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-permutation (P(n,k)) — definition and product formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-permutation of an n-element set is a non-repetitive length-k list made from elements of the set. The number of k-permutations is P(n,k) = n(n − 1)(n − 2) · · · (n − k + 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory examples: P(4,2)=4·3=12, P(4,0)=1 (the empty list), and P(n,k)=0 whenever k>n (no non-repetitive lists longer than n). The i-th position has n−i+1 choices. Demonstrated via small examples listing all k-permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-permutation factorial formula: P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)!
rubrics_metrics.description: For 0 ≤ k ≤ n, P(n,k) = n!/(n − k)! (equivalent to the product formula by extending with cancellation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for quick computation and to connect full permutations (P(n,n)=n!) to partial permutations. Examples: P(8,5) computed both as product 8·7·6·5·4 and as 8!/3! = 6720. Shows P(10,11)=0 because an 11th factor becomes 0 in product formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 3.2 — Binomial coefficient (n choose k)
rubrics_metrics.description: (n choose k) (also C(n,k)) denotes the number of k-element subsets that can be made by choosing k elements from an n-element set. Read as "n choose k."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table examples for small n show how this counts subsets regardless of order. Special cases: (n choose k)=0 if k<0 or k>n, (n choose 0)=1, (n choose n)=1. The notation is the basis for counting combinations like poker hands and lottery tickets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination formula: (n choose k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) (Fact 3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 ≤ k ≤ n, then (n choose k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!). Otherwise (n choose k) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by counting k-permutations and dividing by the k! permutations of each k-element subset (table argument). Examples: (5 choose 3) = 5!/(3!2!) = 10; number of 5-card poker hands = (52 choose 5) = 2,598,960. Used to compute combinations with component selection (e.g., 2 clubs and 3 hearts gives (13 choose 2)(13 choose 3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between permutations and combinations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: each k-element subset can be arranged in k! ways to form k-permutations. This identity is used in the derivation of the combination formula and practical counting translations between ordered and unordered selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry of binomial coefficients: (n choose k) = (n choose n−k)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 0 ≤ k ≤ n, the kth entry of Row n equals the (n − k)th entry: (n choose k) = (n choose n − k) (Equation 3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial explanation: choosing k elements to include is equivalent to choosing n−k elements to exclude. Observed as symmetry in Pascal's triangle and used to simplify computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's Identity (Equation 3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (n+1 choose k) = (n choose k−1) + (n choose k) for integers n,k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial proof: count k-element subsets of {0,1,...,n} by whether they contain 0 or not. This recurrence is the constructive rule for building Pascal's triangle (place 1's at ends, each interior entry is sum of two above). Used to generate binomial coefficients without factorials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's triangle — construction and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange binomial coefficients (n choose k) in rows indexed by n (Row 0 at top). Each number (other than 1) equals the sum of the two numbers immediately above it; Row n lists (n choose 0), (n choose 1), ..., (n choose n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Row entries are the binomial coefficients and correspond to coefficients of (x+y)^n. Examples: Row 7 = 1 7 21 35 35 21 7 1; triangle extends indefinitely. Useful for quick lookup of coefficients and demonstrating symmetry and recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial Theorem (Theorem 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-negative integer n, (x + y)^n = Σ_{k=0}^n (n choose k) x^{n−k} y^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that coefficients of (x+y)^n are the entries of Row n of Pascal's triangle. Examples: (x+y)^7 expanded using row 7; used to compute polynomial expansions and derive identities (e.g., sum_{k=0}^n (n choose k)=2^n). The theorem is accepted here and left to be proven in an exercise later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by case decomposition (use of combinatorial partitioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break a counting task into mutually exclusive cases based on an invariant (e.g., number of 1's in a binary string, how many even elements chosen), count each case, and sum the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in examples: counting 7-digit binary strings with an odd number of 1's by summing counts for 1,3,5,7 ones; counting k-element subsets with exactly r even elements by choosing evens and odds separately and multiplying. Emphasizes choosing positions or counts first, then elements.
